transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-03-10
Time: 15:00 UTC (45m scheduled, we ran 52m)
Duration: 52 minutes
Attendees: Jordan Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Patel (Redwood SE), Aisha Rahman (CTO, Nimbus), Tom Becker (Lead ML Engineer, Nimbus), Ravi Shah (Platform, Nimbus)
Artifacts referenced: benchmark-spreadsheet.xlsx, poc-runbook.md, github.com/redwood/poc-adapter (placeholder)

Summary:
Quick scoping call to align on PoC acceptance criteria, what Nimbus' scripts look like, how we plug the client adapter into Redwood's benchmark harness, and decide streaming vs non-streaming approach for the acceptance benchmarks. Short timeline agreed for draft adapter and dry-run.

Topics covered:
- What constitutes success for the POC (latency SLOs, p95/p99, throughput)
- Workload characterization (qps, payload size, prompt length distribution)
- Harness integration: customer scripts vs Redwood adapter, data sanitization, auth
- Streaming vs non-streaming tradeoffs for latency and cost
- Environment constraints (VPC, KMS, compliance)
- Next steps and owners

Action items (read out in call):
- Priya to build client-adapter prototype and share PR by 2027-03-17
- Jordan to share benchmark spreadsheet and POC runbook by 2027-03-12
- Tom to deliver representative traffic slice + annotated latency-critical examples by 2027-03-19
- Ravi to confirm network constraints and egress IPs by 2027-03-16

Transcript body:
[00:00] Jordan Chen: All right everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood, AE. Priya from our infra team is here too. How's week lookin for Nimbus?
[00:12] Aisha Rahman: Hey Jordan, thanks. Busy but good. We wanna make sure this POC shows we can hit real-time triage for our clinical routing use case, so latency is the big one.
[00:22] Tom Becker: Yeah, ideally we want p95 under 300ms for short prompts, and p99 under a second, below one second for our alert path.
[00:30] Priya Patel: Cool, that's helpful. Quick question on payloads — are most of your requests single-turn short prompts or longer context?
[00:38] Tom Becker: Mix. About 70% short (<64 tokens), 25% medium (64-512), 5% long (512+). The long ones are batch-analysis jobs not in the fast path.
[00:47] Ravi Shah: Also note we have encrypted PHI in some fields. We'll need to confirm whether anything crosses Redwood hosted or stays in our VPC.
[00:55] Jordan Chen: Understood. We can do Private deploy or Dedicated depending on constraints. For the initial bench we can run in Redwood hosted with scrubbed data, then move to a VPC dry-run.
[01:06] Aisha Rahman: Scrubbing works. Tom can annotate examples. We also have auth via SAML SSO and client mTLS for internal services.
[01:15] Priya Patel: Good to know. For the harness, we typically ask for a 48h traffic slice and a set of customer scripts that exercise the main code paths. Two ways to integrate: 1) Redwood adapter wraps your script and calls our SDK, 2) you run your client against our harness endpoints — adapter is easier for us to instrument.
[01:32] Tom Becker: I'm partial to running our existing scripts to avoid rewriting. But we can add a thin shim. How invasive is the adapter?
[01:38] Priya Patel: Usually a 100-200 line shim that maps your client calls to our harness format. We'll share a template. There will be small changes for streaming.
[01:48] Jordan Chen: Also want to call out cost/throughput tradeoffs — streaming reduces perceived latency but can increase ops complexity and can change batching behavior.
[01:57] Aisha Rahman: For triage, perceived latency matters more than token cost. We want streaming if it buys us consistent p95.
[02:04] Tom Becker: On the other hand, streaming can complicate capture for QA. Does Redwood capture partial tokens in the harness?
[02:11] Priya Patel: Yes, we capture the deltas and metrics, but we sometimes see slightly higher tail latency for streaming due to chunking. We can instrument both modes.
[02:18] Ravi Shah: Network wise, our VPC has strict egress rules — we'll need to whitelabel Redwood IPs and use our proxy.
[02:25] Jordan Chen: Okay we'll coordinate on egress IPs. We'll need Ravi's list so our infra team can ensure connectivity.
[02:32] Tom Becker: For success criteria, besides p95/p99, we need throughput target: sustained 120 RPS at 50ms median for the micro service? Wait, that sounds off—maybe 120 RPS at the peak.
[02:44] Jordan Chen: Let's clarify: 120 RPS peak for the short prompt path, with p95 < 300ms and p99 < 1s. We'll capture token-level cost too.
[02:54] Tom Becker: Yes that aligns. Also cold-start tail: we often see spikes during deploy windows. Want to include a cold-start scenario in the bench.
[03:02] Priya Patel: We'll include cold-starts and burst patterns in the harness. We'll simulate a deploy by bringing a node down and spiking traffic.
[03:09] Aisha Rahman: How long for a baseline bench and then a VPC dry-run?
[03:14] Jordan Chen: Baseline hosted bench with scrubbed data — 2 weeks for setup/dry run, then a 48-72h run for acceptance. VPC dry-run depends on networking but we can slot it in the week after if egress is quick.
[03:26] Ravi Shah: That timeline sounds fine if we can get the egress IPs rapidly.
[03:30] Tom Becker: One more on quantization — we plan to run 8-bit quantized variants in prod for cost reasons. Will Redwood's runtime support our quant model or do we need specific build?
[03:40] Priya Patel: We support multiple quant profiles; we'll document recommended model variants. For POC we can test float16 and a quant variant to measure quality delta. Our Optimize module gives recommendations based on observed workload.
[03:52] Jordan Chen: We'll add a tab in the spreadsheet for model variants and expected throughput/latency tradeoffs.
[03:57] Aisha Rahman: About SLAs — we just need confidence the setup can meet the SLOs. We're not negotiating a commercial SLA in the POC phase.
[04:04] Jordan Chen: Totally. POC acceptance criteria will be operational: meets p95/p99 and shows stable throughput across 48h. Commercial SLA discussions happen once we pass POC.
[04:12] Tom Becker: On instrumentation, we need token-level cost attribution and per-route latency breakdown. Does Redwood's console expose that?
[04:20] Priya Patel: Yes, we can surface per-route, per-model metrics and top contributors. We'll attach sample screenshots in the runbook.
[04:26] Ravi Shah: For compliance, we need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. Is there a forwarding option?
[04:32] Jordan Chen: Yes, we can push logs to your collector or share logs with masked content. We'll send our log forwarding guide.
[04:39] Aisha Rahman: Great. Ok can we talk a little about failure modes? We saw another vendor fall back to a smaller model which broke output format. Is Redwood able to do model fallbacks safely?
[04:50] Priya Patel: We support automated fallback policies, with optional validation rules. For structured outputs we recommend a canary run and automated checks on output schema before promoting fallback.
[04:58] Tom Becker: That's good. For the harness we'll want synthetic checks that validate output shape.
[05:04] Jordan Chen: We'll include a sample JSON-schema test in the harness.
[05:09] Aisha Rahman: Regarding the adapter, is it okay if we keep internal auth tokens and the adapter uses short-lived credentials?
[05:17] Priya Patel: Absolutely. We can support short-lived tokens and mTLS. If we're doing VPC, we can also do private peering and no public egress.
[05:25] Tom Becker: On instrumentation again, do you capture streaming chunk timestamps? We've had issues reconciling user timing when chunking occurs.
[05:33] Priya Patel: We timestamp chunks, and we also capture first-byte and final-byte latencies. That lets you compute perceived latency separately from completion latency.
[05:40] Ravi Shah: One nit: our scripts currently use an in-house client that doesn't support incremental consumption. We can either modify it or run a shim. Which is faster?
[05:48] Priya Patel: For speed, we recommend shim/adapter. Modifying a production client takes more time. Adapter approach has low risk.
[05:55] Jordan Chen: We'll provide the adapter template and a working example for node/python.
[06:01] Tom Becker: When you say "adapter template" — is that in the repo or a zip?
[06:04] Priya Patel: We'll post a github PR with a skeleton and tests. We'll also include a script to validate the mapping.
[06:11] Aisha Rahman: For acceptance we'll want a runbook that lists exact commands to reproduce the bench. Can you make that reproducible for our ops folks?
[06:19] Jordan Chen: Yes, that's the runbook (poc-runbook.md). It has steps: 1) prep traffic slice, 2) setup env, 3) run harness with parameters, 4) collect artifacts.
[06:28] Tom Becker: One more ask — can we record per-request model-id so we can tie outputs to model variants?
[06:33] Priya Patel: Yes, we can add a metadata field in the harness to include model id, quant profile, and node-id.
[06:39] Ravi Shah: On the benchmark spreadsheet, what fields should we fill?
[06:42] Jordan Chen: We'll send the template but key fields: request type, avg prompt length, tokens per response, expected p95 target, expected peak RPS, success criteria pass/fail thresholds, and which scenarios are streaming/non-streaming.
[06:54] Tom Becker: Ok we'll populate that for the short prompt path and the medium path.
[06:58] Aisha Rahman: Any blockers from Redwood side?
[07:00] Priya Patel: None technical. We just need the scripts and egress IPs. Also want to confirm whether you'll allow instrumented partial payloads for scrubbed PHI.
[07:09] Tom Becker: We'll scrub PHI, annotate fields as redacted, should be fine.
[07:13] Jordan Chen: Great. Timeline recap: Jordan sends runbook+spreadsheet by 2027-03-12. Priya posts adapter skeleton by 2027-03-17. Nimbus provides traffic slice and IPs by 2027-03-19/16. Dry-run week of 2027-03-22.
[07:28] Aisha Rahman: That works. Can we also schedule a 30m dry-run prep session for the adapter?
[07:33] Jordan Chen: Yes let's pencil in a 30m slot the week of 3/22. We'll send a calendar invite.
[07:39] Tom Becker: Quick question — are we doing streaming for the short prompt path and non-streaming for medium?
[07:45] Priya Patel: That's the recommended split: streaming for short low-latency path, non-streaming for medium where latency is less critical and batching improves cost. We'll validate both.
[07:53] Ravi Shah: Any examples of telemetry we can see?
[07:56] Priya Patel: We'll attach console screenshots (token maps, p95/p99 charts) in the runbook.
[08:02] Aisha Rahman: Ok folks, thanks. This was helpful.
[08:06] Jordan Chen: Thanks everyone. We'll follow up with materials and the invite.

End of call.

Post-call notes (informal):
- Customer strongly emphasizes perceived latency for short prompts (triage path).
- They have strict network egress rules; VPC dry-run likely required for final acceptance.
- Preferred approach: adapter shim to avoid modifying production client; Redwood will supply template.
- Bench acceptance will be 48-72h run with p95/p99 and throughput stability; include cold-start tests and model variant comparisons (float16 vs quant).
